Both patients share the same urgent basic-need (survival).  Care ethics therefore asks whether Ada can meet that need with (1) attentiveness to dependency, (2) responsibility for it, (3) competent action, and (4) responsiveness to the person’s own trust.  
• Competence: The only available treatment works far better for Ben (95 % vs 5 %) [PROP:WORLD:E2, PROP:WORLD:E4].  Care that knowingly offers a 5 % chance when a 95 % chance is available is a serious failure of the competence phase, because it withholds a life-saving benefit that the carer has the power to deliver.
• Promise / trust: Ada’s promise to Cara [PROP:WORLD:RECOGNITION:4697fd89cd506cc4] does generate a responsive obligation; breaking it strains trust.  But in Tronto’s sequence, responsiveness does not license ignoring responsibility and competence.  A promise that directly conflicts with a vastly more competent life-saving act is itself morally defective and must be revised rather than kept.

record.framework_commitment: We rely on Tronto’s four-phase care model: responsibility must be executed competently; responsiveness cannot override responsibility when doing so would knowingly sacrifice a life that could almost certainly be saved.
record.reasoning_bridge: Because the need (survival) and immediacy are identical, the dimension that discriminates the quality of care is competence.  The promise counts, but an imprudent promise cannot transform an incompetent 5 % treatment into the better care option.
record.remaining_uncertainty: Care theory does not offer a precise numerical threshold for when promise-keeping outweighs competence.  If Cara’s chance approached Ben’s, or if additional relational factors (e.g. long-standing dependency) were established, the balance could shift.
record.reversal_condition: If Cara’s survival probability rose to roughly match Ben’s (≥ 90 %), or if the scenario established a unique, long-term entrusted care relationship to Cara that Ben lacks, A1 would become preferable.
